title: Operation Chromite & the Recapture of Seoul (1950): The 5,000-to-1 Gamble
subtitle: September 15 – 28, 1950

lines: Dawn, September 15th, 1950. The sea off Inchon, Korea.
In the darkness, more than two hundred and sixty ships lay waiting in silence, their crews holding their breath.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: But this was a strange and treacherous sea. A sea that vanished twice a day.
When the tide went out, up to four kilometers of mudflats lay bare in front of the shore.
Ships could reach the shore only for two or three hours around high tide.
Miss that window, and the landing force would be stranded on the mud.
The man who pushed for this operation: Douglas MacArthur, Commander-in-Chief of the United Nations Command.
It was a gamble so risky it came to be called a five-thousand-to-one shot.
And the gamble paid off in a single day.
Yet something strange followed. From Inchon to Seoul was barely thirty kilometers.
And retaking Seoul would take thirteen full days.
For the Marines who crossed the sea, the real hell was waiting in Seoul.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: The Inchon Landing and the Recapture of Seoul.
This is the story of a five-thousand-to-one gamble, and thirteen days of street fighting.
June 25th, 1950. A surprise North Korean invasion began the war.
Seoul fell in just three days, and South Korean and American troops were pushed south, and further south, week after week.
By August, all that remained was a narrow corner east of the Naktong River.

callouts.text: AUG. 1950 · DRIVEN BACK TO THE NAKTONG

lines: This last line, with its back to Pusan, was called the Pusan Perimeter.
By late August, North Korea was preparing a final all-out offensive to break it.
One more breach, and South Korea would be pushed into the sea.
On September 1st, North Korea struck along the entire Naktong front.
From Yongsan to Tabu-dong, from Yongchon to Pohang, the line began to crack.
The defenders survived only by rushing their last reserves from one breach to the next, day and night.
Meanwhile, at UN headquarters in Tokyo, a very different plan was taking shape.
Land a massive force far behind enemy lines, at the port of Inchon, the gateway to Seoul.
Its name was Operation Chromite.

visual.head: OPERATION CHROMITE
rows: OBJECTIVE: LAND AT INCHON, RETAKE SEOUL

lines: MacArthur reportedly first imagined this plan just four days into the war.
Watching Seoul burn from a hill south of the Han, he pictured a blow to the enemy's rear.
A landing planned in July had to be shelved for lack of troops, but he never let go of Inchon.
scenes.label: MacArthur on an inspection tour of the Korean front (1950)

lines: The idea was simple.
Every North Korean supply line ran south through Seoul.
Cut that lifeline, and the entire enemy army fighting at the Naktong would be trapped, with no food, no ammunition, and no way home.
But Washington's response was cold.
On August 23rd, the Army and Navy chiefs of staff flew to Tokyo for a conference.
One by one, Navy officers reported that Inchon had nearly every natural condition that makes an amphibious landing fail.
scenes.label: MacArthur greets Army Chief Collins and Navy Chief Sherman in Tokyo (Aug. 1950)

lines: Tides, mudflats, a narrow channel, a fortress island, and high seawalls.
Some even proposed a safer landing farther south, on the open beaches near Kunsan.
MacArthur answered with a long, passionate speech.
Because everyone believed a landing there was impossible, he argued, the enemy would never be ready for it.
The room fell silent, and the operation was approved.
D-Day was September 15th. Barely three weeks away.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: Why was Inchon so dangerous? The map tells the story.
From the open sea to Inchon harbor, there was only one narrow channel between islands and shoals.
Its name: Flying Fish Channel.
Currents reached up to eight knots, nearly fifteen kilometers an hour.
One sunken ship or a single mine in that channel could leave the whole fleet behind it stranded and helpless.
But the greatest enemy was the sea itself. The tidal range reached about nine meters.
That's like the height of a three-story building, rising and falling twice a day.
At low tide, landing craft stuck fast in the mud, and the men inside became easy targets on open ground.

visual.title: Inchon Tidal Cross-Section
visual.note: Schematic · range: ~9 m (Korean sources) / Sept. 15 predicted high tide 31.5 ft (USMC)

lines: Only a few days a month brought tides high enough to reach the seawalls.
Miss September 15th, and the next chance came in mid-October, when the cold was setting in.
And right in front of the harbor stood a fortress island: Wolmi-do.
Unless Wolmi-do fell first, the main force would expose its flank the moment it entered the port.
But between the attack on Wolmi-do and the main landing, the ebb tide left a gap of nearly twelve hours.
Wolmi-do would be taken on the morning tide, and the main force would land only on the evening tide.
That was more than enough time for the enemy to guess exactly where the main landing would come, and to rush in reinforcements.

visual.sub: Morning tide → Wolmi-do · Evening tide → Inchon beaches

lines: Deceiving the enemy mattered just as much.
UN forces bombed and shelled Kunsan and the east coast, faking landings elsewhere.
Two days before the landing, destroyers sailed right up to Wolmi-do to draw the enemy's fire.
The moment those guns fired back, their carefully hidden positions were revealed, and the warships destroyed them.
So before the landing, someone had to go into those waters first.
In mid-August, South Korean naval intelligence agents, disguised as fishermen, slipped onto Yonghung-do island.
Water depth, mud firmness, gun positions, seawall heights. They measured it all by hand.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: From September 1st, U.S. Navy Lieutenant Eugene Clark's team also operated from the island.
Night after night, their reports filled in Tokyo's invasion maps, piece by piece, and the plan took shape.
But on September 14th, one day before the landing, North Korean troops raided Yonghung-do.
Lieutenant Im Byeong-rae and Petty Officer Hong Si-uk stayed behind to cover their comrades' escape.
Refusing to be taken prisoner, both men met their end on that island.
scenes.label: Dramatization

callouts.text: SEPT. 14, 1950 · LT. IM BYEONG-RAE & PO HONG SI-UK KILLED

lines: Then, around midnight on September 15th, the dark Palmi-do lighthouse blazed to life.
Agents had climbed the island and relit it, and its beam guided the fleet into the narrow channel.
Now, the hour of no return was approaching.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: At dawn on September 15th, the fleet's guns opened up on Wolmi-do.
After several days of bombing and napalm, the little island was already a burning mountain of shattered rock.
Cruisers, destroyers, and Marine Corsair fighters took turns pounding it.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: On the bridge of the flagship Mount McKinley stood the seventy-year-old MacArthur.
Watching through his binoculars, he knew the first card of his great gamble was about to be played.
scenes.label: MacArthur watching the landing aboard USS Mount McKinley (Sept. 15, 1950)

lines: At 6:33 a.m., the 3rd Battalion, 5th Marines, landed on Wolmi-do's northwest shore.
On the invasion maps, it was marked in green: Green Beach.
Nine M26 Pershing tanks came ashore with them.
Stunned by the bombardment, the North Korean positions collapsed faster than expected.
At 6:55, just twenty-two minutes after landing, Marines planted the Stars and Stripes on the summit.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: By about eight o'clock, Wolmi-do was completely in Marine hands.
Over a hundred North Koreans were killed and a hundred thirty-six captured. Not a single Marine was killed.
Prisoners revealed the island had been held by a coastal artillery regiment and part of a marine regiment.
The defenders of Inchon itself appeared to number fewer than two thousand.
And the enemy still wasn't even sure whether this was the real landing, or just another feint.
scenes.label: North Koreans surrendering on Wolmi-do (Sept. 15, 1950)

lines: But the triumph was brief. The sea began draining away fast.
Between Wolmi-do and the harbor, an endless plain of mud appeared.
The Marine battalion on the island was now cut off, alone, without the main force.
Had the enemy rolled tanks across the causeway, they could have been trapped.
And so began the long, long wait for the evening tide.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: In the afternoon, the sea began rising again.
Around 5:30 p.m., landing craft raced toward the Inchon shore in two waves.
The 5th Marines at Red Beach to the north, the 1st Marines at Blue Beach to the south.
Red Beach was no beach at all. It was a stone seawall taller than a man.
The Marines had to throw ladders against it from their boats and climb.
And just beyond that wall, North Korean machine guns and grenades were waiting for them.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: This photograph was actually taken at Red Beach that day.
The man going over the wall at the top of the ladder is platoon leader, First Lieutenant Baldomero Lopez.
Minutes later, wounded and unable to throw a grenade, he smothered it with his own body to save his men.
scenes.label: Lt. Lopez scaling the Red Beach seawall (Sept. 15, 1950)

lines: Before sunset, the Marines took Cemetery Hill and Observatory Hill behind the beach.
By nightfall, a solid beachhead stood atop the seawall, and more men and guns were pouring ashore.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: South Korean Marines were also at Red Beach.
Back to reclaim their homeland, they swept into Inchon's streets, hunting down hidden enemy troops.
Their fight, begun on this shore, would carry them into the heart of Seoul thirteen days later.
scenes.label: ROK Marines searching North Korean prisoners (Sept. 1950)

lines: At Blue Beach to the south, the Marines met a different enemy.
Smoke, darkness, and mud that gripped their ankles.
Some boats landed in the wrong places, but the 1st Marines fought their way ashore.
That evening, eight big LST landing ships deliberately ran aground at Red Beach.
Knowing the ebb tide would trap them in the mud, they unloaded ammunition and gear all night.
scenes.label: LSTs high and dry at low tide on Red Beach (Sept. 16, 1950)

lines: On the first day, twenty-one UN troops were killed.
Far fewer than the planners had feared for such a dangerous landing. Almost unbelievably few.
The next day, September 16th, ROK Marines cleared the last enemy troops from Inchon.
In just one day, the five-thousand-to-one gamble had turned the tide of the entire war.
But the road ahead to Seoul would prove far rougher, and far bloodier, than the sea.
From Inchon, two roads led to Seoul.
The 5th Marines headed north to Kimpo Airfield. The 1st Marines drove down the highway toward Yongdungpo.
They had to reach the Han River before North Korea could reinforce the defenses of Seoul.
Dawn, September 17th. A pass near Ascom City.
Out of the fog came six North Korean T-34 tanks, carrying infantry.
They had no idea that Marines were lying in wait on the low hill just ahead of them.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: The Marines waited until the tanks were right on top of them.
Then bazookas, recoilless rifles, and the Pershings' 90-millimeter guns all fired at once.
Within minutes, all six T-34s were in flames.
About two hundred North Korean infantry fell with them, while the records list just one Marine wounded.
That day, MacArthur came ashore at Inchon to see the front himself.
Standing on that still-smoking road beside the burnt-out tanks, he urged a faster drive on Seoul.
scenes.label: MacArthur and Col. Puller at the front (Sept. 17, 1950)

lines: On the morning of September 18th, the 5th Marines took Kimpo Airfield.
Transport planes began landing almost at once, opening a supply route to Seoul by air.
The North Koreans didn't give up easily.
Through that night and dawn, they launched counterattack after counterattack to retake the runway.
But the Marines threw back every one from their foxholes, and the enemy fell back toward the Han.
Meanwhile, on the highway, the 1st Marines were stopped in front of Yongdungpo.
Yongdungpo was Seoul's southern gateway, and the enemy had made it a fortress.
Across the stream dikes, fierce fighting raged for more than two days.
On September 21st, Captain Robert Barrow's Able Company slipped through a gap into the heart of Yongdungpo.
That night, five T-34 tanks rolled toward them.
Cut off, the company fought back with bazookas and beat off five assaults through the night.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: At daybreak, some two hundred North Korean dead lay in front of their position.
On September 22nd, Yongdungpo finally fell to the Marines.
Now only one great obstacle stood between the Marines and Seoul: the wide Han River.
Most of the Han River bridges had been destroyed early in the war.
The only way into the capital was straight across the water, under the enemy's guns.
On the night of September 19th, Marine reconnaissance swimmers crossed first near Haengju.
But machine guns opened up from the far bank, and the scouts had to pull back.
The next morning at 6:45, the 5th Marines climbed into LVT amphibious tractors.
The same vehicles that had crossed the sea at Inchon now charged across the river.
During the crossing, the tractors took more than two hundred hits.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: The Marines stormed Hill 125 across the river and took it by 9:40 a.m.
Taking that one hill cost a single company forty-three casualties.
By that afternoon, a solid bridgehead stood firmly on the north bank of the Han.
ROK Marine battalions crossed alongside the 5th Marines.
On the 21st, the newly arrived 7th Marines landed at Inchon and rushed to the front.
Day by day, the bridgehead north of the Han grew.
But at Seoul's western edge, the enemy was waiting.
A chain of low hills ran from Ansan through Yonhui to Wau-san.
Along this ridge, North Korea dug in and built its last line of defense for the capital.

callouts.text: NK WESTERN DEFENSE LINE OF SEOUL (APPROX.)

lines: At first, Seoul's defenders were thought to number around five thousand.
But with the 18th Division turned back from the Naktong, they swelled to over twenty thousand.
Ansan, the highest, stood two hundred ninety-six meters. Yonhui Ridge below it, one hundred four.
They were not high, but they looked down over open rice paddies and streets below. A natural fortress.
From September 22nd, U.S. and South Korean Marines hit this ridge head-on.
Bunkers laced with machine guns and mortars changed hands again and again.
The ROK Marines' 1st Battalion, assigned to Hill 104, paid a heavy price.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: On September 24th alone, the 1st Marine Division suffered two hundred eighty-five casualties.
It was the bloodiest single day of the entire battle for Seoul.

visual.sub: Sept. 24, 1950 · 1st Marine Division casualties (highest of the Seoul battle)

lines: After three days and nights of slaughter, the hills along the ridge fell one by one.
The western gate to Seoul was finally starting to open.
On September 24th, the 1st Marines also crossed the Han into southwest Seoul.
Before dawn the next day, the U.S. 32nd Infantry and ROK 17th Regiment crossed farther east.
And at 3 p.m., the 32nd seized Namsan, in the very heart of Seoul.
That night, X Corps commander Major General Edward Almond announced that Seoul had been liberated.
It was September 25th, exactly three months after the war began.
Yet even as he spoke, gunfire still echoed through the streets of the city.
scenes.label: Almond (left), MacArthur and others at a briefing at the Marine division CP, Inchon (Sept. 17, 1950)

lines: North Korea had blocked every major street in Seoul with barricades.
Rice bags filled with earth, stacked higher than a man.
Behind them hid anti-tank guns and machine guns. In front, the road was mined.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: On the main boulevards, a wall like this appeared every two to three hundred meters.
Each took forty-five minutes on average to break, as the Marines retook Seoul block by block.

visual.sub: Main boulevards · ~45 min to clear each (USMC records)

lines: And in the middle of those streets were the people of Seoul.
More than a million residents are thought to have been unable to flee three months earlier.
Hiding in cellars and air raid shelters, they listened to the shells passing overhead and waited, hoping to survive until liberation.
scenes.label: UN troops fighting in the streets of Seoul (Sept. 1950)

lines: First, aircraft and mortars pounded the wall. Then tanks moved up to knock out the anti-tank guns.
Engineers cleared the mines, and infantry advanced, searching every building.
Snipers could be hiding behind any roof or window, so no one could relax for a single step.
Meanwhile, street after street of the old capital was swallowed by fire and smoke.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: Before dawn on September 26th, about a thousand North Korean troops counterattacked Namsan.
The 32nd Infantry held, keeping the high ground in the heart of the city.
Then, at dawn on September 27th, the Marines finally reached the Capitol.
The old Japanese Government-General Building, where South Korea's government had sat.
ROK Marine platoon leader Park Jeong-mo and his men tore down the North Korean flag and raised the Taegukgi.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: Three months after Seoul fell, the South Korean flag flew there once more.
That same day, U.S. Marines raised the Stars and Stripes over the old American and Soviet embassies.
scenes.label: U.S. Marines raise the flag at the American Consulate in Seoul (Sept. 1950)

lines: On September 28th, the Marines took the last hills north of Seoul.
Thirteen days after the Inchon landing, Seoul was fully back in friendly hands.
At noon the next day, September 29th, a ceremony restoring the capital was held at the Capitol.
MacArthur told President Syngman Rhee he was returning Seoul to him.
Glass from the shell-shattered roof fell throughout his speech.
scenes.label: MacArthur leads the Lord's Prayer at the Seoul ceremony (Sept. 29, 1950)

lines: With Seoul gone, the North Korean army on the Naktong was suddenly cut off.
The U.S. Eighth Army and ROK forces, attacking from September 16th, drove north in just ten days.
On September 26th, near Osan, UN forces from north and south finally linked up.

callouts.text: SUPPLY LINE CUT → NAKTONG FRONT COLLAPSES (APPROX.)

lines: Without supplies or a road home, North Korean troops threw down their weapons by the thousands and fled into the hills.
From Inchon to Seoul, UN and South Korean casualties numbered about three thousand five hundred.
X Corps estimated about fourteen thousand North Koreans killed and some seven thousand captured.

visual.note: Inchon–Seoul operation · UN: total casualties / NK: U.S. X Corps estimate

lines: One landing at Inchon completely reversed the course of the war.
After three months of retreat, it was now the UN's turn to drive north.
But this sweeping victory would soon bring a new enemy across the Yalu.

callouts.text: AFTER INCHON · THE DRIVE NORTH, AND CHINA'S SHADOW (APPROX.)

lines: So why did a landing that succeeded in one day take thirteen days to reach Seoul?
Let's look closely at four reasons.

visual.head: 1 Day at Sea vs 13 Days in Seoul

lines: First: the Han River, a giant moat.
With the bridges down, the Marines had to cross the river in tractors and boats.
Gathering enough crossing equipment and securing bridgeheads under fire ate up several precious days.
Second: a swelling garrison.
Hearing of the landing, North Korea even turned back units headed south, and poured troops into Seoul.
The closer the Marines came to the city, the more defenders stood in their way.
scenes.label: U.S. Marines in the street fighting for Seoul (Sept. 1950)

lines: Third: a double wall of ridges and barricades.
Once at Ansan and Yonhui Ridge, and again at the barricades downtown.
The enemy wrapped Seoul in two walls of defense, and demanded blood for every single step forward.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: Fourth: a command in a hurry.
Almond drove his units hard, determined to retake Seoul on the three-month anniversary.
He clashed sharply with 1st Marine Division commander General Oliver Smith over where to cross the Han.
The three days between that hasty announcement and the real recapture show the true weight of this battle.
If the single day at Inchon was a victory of daring surprise,
the thirteen days in Seoul were a victory won block by block, in blood.

visual.title: What Inchon and Seoul Left Behind

items.text: One day of surprise at sea
Thirteen days of blood in Seoul

lines: Coming out after three months, the people of Seoul waved flags they had kept hidden.
But much of the city they returned to was already in ruins and ashes.
Countless people had lost their homes, and countless more had lost their families.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: From the fierce channels off Inchon to the narrow alleys of Seoul.
In those thirteen days, countless names fell, many of them never to be remembered.
Today, a lighthouse still stands on Palmi-do, shining over the sea off Inchon.
We hope you'll remember, just once, those who risked their lives for that light.
